note: Russia splits the period across two forms rather than one, and the split is the point: the KS-2 act records what was accepted and the KS-3 certificate records what it is worth cumulatively. That maps onto the spine without a new sentence because the spine already separates the document that states the value from the document that asks for the money.
title: Close the month with a KS-2 act and a KS-3 certificate
desc: Measure the period against the smeta, expand the GESN norms into the resources they carry, get the KS-2 act signed by the client's technical supervisor and raise the KS-3 certificate against it, so the cumulative figure and the accepted figure never disagree.
longDesc: The KS-2 and the KS-3 answer two different questions and a great deal of month-end argument comes from treating them as one document in two copies. The KS-2 is the act of acceptance: it lists what was executed, position by position, at the rates the smeta carries, and it is signed by the party who accepted it. The KS-3 is cumulative: it states the value of the works from the beginning of the contract to this period, which is what the payment is calculated from. A KS-3 that does not follow from the KS-2 acts behind it is a reconciliation nobody can complete, and it surfaces at the worst moment, when the contract closes and the totals have to agree.

slots.clockStart: the day the KS-2 act is signed
slots.escalationRoute: send the pretenziya and start the contractual penalty running

note.what: A norm-based rate carries the labour, machinery and materials behind it, so the act can be read back to the resources it claims rather than to a single figure. That is what makes a disagreement about one position a conversation about one norm.

in.label: Amount accepted on the KS-2 acts

note.why: The two forms are reconciled at contract close whether or not anybody reconciled them monthly, and a year of small differences is not a month of arithmetic. Doing it every period is the same work spread over the time when it is still cheap to correct.
